passage:
Bidisha, in Class 11, pinned her whole week to the wall: school, three coaching batches, bus rides, homework. She added it up with a pencil and stared at the total: sixty-two hours, and not one for rest. She was not lazy; the week was simply too full.

She compared her batches. Two of them explained ideas she had not understood at school; the third repeated the school lesson. She dropped the third, and the hours it freed went into working problems alone and sleeping properly.

Irfan kept all his batches because Kamal and the others did. He sat in chairs from morning to nine at night. His notebooks were full, but he could not remember the lectures, and his test marks stayed flat month after month.

Noticing a heavy, grey feeling every afternoon, Bidisha added two lines to her calendar in pen: a thirty-minute walk, and Sunday afternoon free. They were as fixed as her classes. When a friend asked whether that was wasted time, she said, "It's what lets the rest stick."

qa.q: How many hours a week did Bidisha's timetable add up to?
qa.a: It added up to sixty-two hours.

qa.q: How did Bidisha's changes to her batches differ from Irfan's habit, and what happened to their results?
qa.a: Bidisha kept the two batches that explained ideas, freeing time to practise and sleep, while Irfan stayed in every batch and his marks stayed flat.

qa.q: What might Irfan feel when his marks stay flat?
qa.a: Discouraged and worn out, since long days bring no visible progress.
Irfan could add up his week, find which batches help most, and free some time for practice and rest.

grounding: Four approaches to coaching overload: auditing the timetable, keeping the batches that help most, attending everything from fear, and scheduling rest and exercise.
